text: American farmers did not lobby for daylight saving time: they led the fight that repealed national daylight saving in 1919, over Wilson's veto. It began as a 1916 German wartime fuel measure. US clocks fell back an hour this morning.

In 1774, three hundred metres of a Paris road dropped into the quarry tunnels beneath it. Twelve years later a disused quarry was consecrated as an ossuary, and carts arrived after dark, loaded with the dead. It is All Souls' Day.

In a Cambridge wind-tunnel film, air over a wing reaches the back edge before air under it. NASA calls the school story that the two meet there "the most popular incorrect theory of lift". Wings stay up by turning air downward.

The 2010 study said to prove the chicken came first was a computer simulation of calcite crystals forming. It dated nothing and examined no fossils. The egg came first, by hundreds of millions of years.

Nobody designed QWERTY to slow typists down. It began in 1868 as a piano-style alphabetical keyboard. A telegraph school advertised the machine as producing letters "faster than the most rapid penman".
A fly that walks across your plate has already sampled it before its mouthparts arrive. Much of its sense of taste and all of its grip live in its feet. Flies rub their legs together to clean them.

Four pet cats have been filmed sitting inside a square that was not there: an illusion made of four Pac-Man shapes taped to the floor, cut-out corners facing inward. They sat in it seven times. A real square outline drew cats eight times.

Nearly every golden hamster in a cage descends from a brother and sister mated in Jerusalem in 1930. They came from a litter dug out of a wheat field near Aleppo, Syria. Wild ones are Endangered, and trapped and poisoned as crop pests.

In its 2000 edition, the US government's own style manual called noon 12 a.m. and midnight 12 p.m. Its 2008 edition reversed both. NIST says 12 a.m. and 12 p.m. "are ambiguous and should not be used."

More red light than blue comes back from synthetic skin above an artificial vein, a 2026 optics study found. The vein reads blue only because the skin beside it returns even more red. Human blood is red at every oxygen level.
For seven years, the federal Veterans Day fell in October. The first "was observed with much confusion" on October 25, 1971, and it went back to November 11 in 1978. Today is Veterans Day.

In 1962, Popular Mechanics called Einstein a man "who never took an intelligence test" and, in the same parenthesis, gave his estimated IQ as 207. There is no record that he ever took one. The famous 160 has no test behind it either.

The real Illuminati used an owl and was outlawed in Bavaria by 1785. The dollar's eye and pyramid come from the Great Seal of 1782, whose official description sets no number of steps: the 13 are a tradition. It is Friday the 13th.

A spotted hyena's giggle often comes from one kept off a kill by higher-ranking clanmates. Researchers read the call as submission and frustration, not amusement. Its pitch can even carry clues to the caller's age.

A capital M set in 12-point type is not 12 points of anything. The em dash was cast one em wide, and an em is a unit equal to the type size. The M that lent the unit its name does not fill the em square.
Alexander Bain, a Scottish clockmaker, patented a fax machine in 1843. Paris was faxing Lyon in 1865, 11 years before Bell patented the telephone. Fax machines filled offices in the 1980s.

A Moon that had stopped rotating would show Earth every side of itself once a month. The real one rotates once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth, roughly 27.3 days, so the same hemisphere stays pointed at Earth.

More than 99% of Earth's gold lies in the core, under about 3,000 km of solid rock. Every gold ring, coin and circuit board ever made came out of the sliver outside it. Most of that gold is thought to have arrived later, on meteorites.

The poop deck is named for the poop, an old word for a ship's stern recorded in English by 1489, two centuries before poop had any bodily sense. The crew's toilets were at the bow. It is World Toilet Day.

Bluetooth was meant to be called PAN, the winner of a 4-1 vote. PAN could not be trademarked, and the backup, RadioWire, had not been searched in time. The stand-in codename, named after a 10th-century Danish king, stuck.

For 52 and a half years, a US federal rule said a television's size, unless the seller said otherwise, meant the width of its picture. The diagonal, the figure every set is sold by, needed a label until 2019. It is World Television Day.

Oregon's famous exploding whale was blown up on purpose, with half a ton of dynamite, by the state Highway Division in 1970. One chunk flattened a parked car a quarter-mile away. "It went just exactly right," the engineer said.

Nobody can write out Graham's number in ordinary digits, but its final digits are known: they end in 4195387. It once held the record for the biggest number in a mathematical proof. It is Fibonacci Day, 11/23.

The two accounts of the 1620 Plymouth landing written by people who were there mention no rock. Plymouth Rock was pointed out about 1741 by a church elder in his nineties, citing his father, who arrived in 1623. It is Thanksgiving week.

Rafter, the trivia answer for a group of turkeys, sounds medieval but has not been traced in print before 1908. Gang was in print by 1709, and flock, the usual word, by 1657. Thanksgiving is tomorrow.

Gram for gram, chicken breast has about as much tryptophan as turkey breast, and parmesan has more. If tryptophan were the reason turkey makes people sleepy, chicken would do the job just as well. Happy Thanksgiving.

In 1890, fourteen resellers in Brest protested in elegant calligraphy when a paper called the town's fair a flea market. The name jeered at secondhand rags believed to carry fleas, and it stuck anyway. It is Black Friday.

Cornell's cat behavior expert rejects the snake theory behind the cucumber videos. Cats have no natural fear of snakes, she said, and many hunt them. In an Australian study, six of 358 feral and stray cats had eaten venomous snakes.

The X in Xmas is not the English letter X but the Greek letter chi, the first letter of Christos. English scribes used it as shorthand for Christ by the 11th century, long before advertising. Advent starts today.
Netscape invented the web cookie in 1994 to make a shopping cart work. The original spec says "the state object is called a cookie, for no compelling reason." It is Cyber Monday.
